maximum-average-subarray-i.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window (add the element that enters, subtract the one that leaves)

approaches.name: Sum every window from scratch
approaches.idea: There are n − k + 1 windows of size k. Add up each one separately and keep the largest sum; the best average is that sum divided by k.
steps: For each start `i` from 0 to n − k, add `nums[i] … nums[i + k − 1]`.
Keep the largest sum seen.
Return the largest sum divided by `k` (as a decimal).
approaches.why: n − k + 1 windows, each summed in O(k). When k is about n/2 that is about n²/4 additions.

approaches.name: Prefix sums
approaches.idea: With `prefix[i]` = sum of the first `i` values, any window sum is a difference of two prefix sums: `prefix[i + k] − prefix[i]`.
steps: Build `prefix` of length n + 1 with `prefix[0] = 0` and `prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]`.
For each start `i`, the window sum is `prefix[i + k] − prefix[i]`; keep the largest.
Return the largest sum divided by `k`.
approaches.why: One pass builds the prefix array and one pass reads n − k + 1 differences. The prefix array costs O(n) memory, which the sliding window avoids.

approaches.name: Slide a window of size k
approaches.idea: Neighbouring windows share k − 1 elements. Moving the window one step adds the new element on the right and removes the one that falls off the left.
steps: Sum the first `k` elements; this is the current and best sum.
For `i` from `k` to n − 1: `sum += nums[i] − nums[i − k]`, then update the best.
Return the best sum divided by `k`.
approaches.why: Each element enters the window once and leaves once, and only the running sum and the best are stored. Dividing only at the end avoids rounding on every step.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.pattern: Variable-size sliding window (grow on the right, shrink on the left while the window is invalid)

approaches.name: From every start, extend until a character repeats
approaches.idea: For each starting index, keep adding characters to a set; the first repeated character ends the longest valid substring from that start.
steps: For each start `i`, create an empty set.
Move `j` from `i` to the right; if `s[j]` is already in the set, stop; otherwise add it.
The substring `s[i..j)` has no repeats; update the best length with `j − i`.
Return the best length.
approaches.why: Each start can scan to the end of the string, giving O(n²) in the worst case. (A scan never runs longer than the alphabet size σ before repeating, so it is really O(n·σ).) The set holds at most σ characters.

approaches.name: Sliding window with a set, shrinking one step at a time
approaches.idea: Keep a window `s[l..r]` with no repeats. When `s[r]` is already inside, remove characters from the left until it is not.
steps: Set `l = 0` and an empty set.
For each `r`: while `s[r]` is in the set, remove `s[l]` and move `l` right.
Add `s[r]`; the window `s[l..r]` has no repeats, so update the best with `r − l + 1`.
Return the best length.
approaches.why: Each character is added once (when `r` reaches it) and removed at most once (when `l` passes it): at most 2n set operations. The set holds at most σ characters.

approaches.name: Sliding window that jumps using the last position of each character
approaches.idea: Remember where each character was last seen. When `s[r]` repeats inside the window, the left edge can jump straight past its previous position instead of stepping there.
steps: Keep `last[c]` = the last index where character `c` appeared (−1 if never), and `l = 0`.
For each `r`: if `last[s[r]] >= l`, the repeat is inside the window, so set `l = last[s[r]] + 1`.
Set `last[s[r]] = r` and update the best with `r − l + 1`.
Return the best length.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) work per character; `l` only moves forward. The table has one entry per possible character (128 for ASCII).

minimum-size-subarray-sum.pattern: Variable-size sliding window on positive numbers (shrink while the window is still valid)

approaches.name: From every start, extend until the sum reaches target
approaches.idea: For each start, add elements until the sum reaches `target`; the first such end gives the shortest subarray from that start.
steps: For each start `i`, set `sum = 0`.
Move `j` right from `i`, adding `nums[j]`; as soon as `sum >= target`, record `j − i + 1` and stop.
Return the smallest length recorded, or 0 if none.
approaches.why: Each start may scan to the end: about n²/2 additions in the worst case.

approaches.name: Prefix sums and binary search
approaches.idea: All values are positive, so prefix sums are strictly increasing. For each start `i`, binary search the first end where `prefix[end] − prefix[i] >= target`.
steps: Build `prefix` with `prefix[0] = 0`, `prefix[k + 1] = prefix[k] + nums[k]`.
For each start `i`, binary search the smallest `e` with `prefix[e] >= prefix[i] + target`.
If such an `e` exists, the subarray `nums[i..e − 1]` has length `e − i`; keep the smallest.
Return the smallest length, or 0.
approaches.why: n binary searches over an array of n + 1 prefix sums. Binary search works only because positive values make the prefix sums sorted.

approaches.name: Sliding window: grow right, shrink left while the sum is enough
approaches.idea: Extend the window to the right; whenever its sum reaches `target`, record the length and shrink from the left as long as the sum stays at or above `target`.
steps: Set `l = 0`, `sum = 0`.
For each `r`, add `nums[r]` to `sum`.
While `sum >= target`: record `r − l + 1`, subtract `nums[l]`, and move `l` right.
Return the smallest length recorded, or 0.
approaches.why: Each index enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the total work is O(n). Positivity is what makes this valid: shrinking can only lower the sum, so once it drops below `target` no shorter window ending at `r` exists.

max-consecutive-ones-iii.pattern: Variable-size sliding window with a budget (at most k zeros inside)

approaches.name: From every start, extend while at most k zeros
approaches.idea: Flipping at most k zeros means finding the longest subarray with at most k zeros. Try every start and extend until a (k + 1)-th zero appears.
steps: For each start `i`, set `zeros = 0`.
Move `j` right; count zeros; stop when `zeros` would exceed `k`.
The run `nums[i..j)` is valid; update the best with `j − i`.
Return the best.
approaches.why: Each start may scan to the end of the array.

approaches.name: Prefix count of zeros and binary search
approaches.idea: `zeros[i]` = number of zeros among the first `i` values never decreases. For each right end `r`, binary search the leftmost start whose window has at most k zeros.
steps: Build `zeros` with `zeros[0] = 0` and `zeros[i + 1] = zeros[i] + (nums[i] == 0 ? 1 : 0)`.
For each `r`, find the smallest `l` with `zeros[r + 1] − zeros[l] <= k`, i.e. `zeros[l] >= zeros[r + 1] − k`.
Update the best with `r − l + 1`.
Return the best.
approaches.why: n binary searches over the n + 1 prefix counts, which are sorted because counts never go down.

approaches.name: Sliding window that keeps at most k zeros
approaches.idea: Grow the window to the right, counting zeros. When there are more than k zeros, move the left edge until one zero leaves.
steps: Set `l = 0`, `zeros = 0`.
For each `r`: if `nums[r] == 0`, increase `zeros`.
While `zeros > k`: if `nums[l] == 0`, decrease `zeros`; move `l` right.
Update the best with `r − l + 1`; return it at the end.
approaches.why: Both edges only move forward, so each index is visited at most twice. Only two indices and a counter are stored.

longest-repeating-character-replacement.pattern: Variable-size sliding window: a window is valid when length − (count of its most common letter) ≤ k

approaches.name: From every start, extend while the window can be fixed
approaches.idea: A substring can become one repeated letter if the letters that are not its most common letter number at most `k`. Try every start and extend, keeping letter counts.
steps: For each start `i`, reset 26 counts and `maxCount = 0`.
Move `j` right: count `s[j]` and update `maxCount`.
If `(j − i + 1) − maxCount <= k`, the window works: update the best length; otherwise stop (longer windows from `i` only need more changes).
Return the best.
approaches.why: Up to n starts, each scanning up to n letters with O(1) work. The 26 counters are constant space.

approaches.name: Sliding window, recomputing the most common letter
approaches.idea: Keep a window and its letter counts. While the window needs more than `k` changes, shrink it from the left; the needed changes are the length minus the largest of the 26 counts.
steps: Set `l = 0` and 26 counts at 0.
For each `r`, count `s[r]`.
While `(r − l + 1) − max(count) > k`, uncount `s[l]` and move `l` right.
Update the best with `r − l + 1`; return it at the end.
approaches.why: Each edge moves at most n times, and each check scans 26 counts.

approaches.name: Sliding window that never lowers the best count
approaches.idea: The answer only grows when some window has a larger most-common count, so `maxCount` never needs to go down. With a stale `maxCount` the window just slides at its best length instead of shrinking.
steps: Set `l = 0`, `maxCount = 0` and 26 counts.
For each `r`: count `s[r]` and set `maxCount = max(maxCount, count[s[r]])`.
If `(r − l + 1) − maxCount > k`, uncount `s[l]` and move `l` right once (the window keeps its length).
Return `n − l` at the end (the final window length, which is the best length seen).
approaches.why: O(1) work per character. The window never shrinks, it only grows or slides; it grows only when a real window with a higher count is found, so its final length is the answer.

permutation-in-string.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window with letter counts (anagram check)

approaches.name: Sort each window and compare
approaches.idea: Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when their sorted letters are equal. Sort `s1` once and compare it with every sorted window of `s2` of the same length.
steps: Let `n = s1.length`; if `n > s2.length`, return false.
Sort the letters of `s1`.
For each start `i` in `s2`, sort `s2[i..i + n)` and compare it with sorted `s1`; return true on a match.
Return false if no window matches.
approaches.why: About m windows (m = `s2.length`), each sorted in O(n log n). Each sorted copy takes O(n) memory.

approaches.name: Slide a window of counts and compare all 26
approaches.idea: Instead of sorting, compare letter counts. Keep counts for the current window of `s2` and update them as it slides: one letter enters and one leaves.
steps: Count the letters of `s1` in `need[26]`.
Slide a window of length n over `s2`, adding the entering letter to `have` and removing the letter that leaves.
Whenever the window has length n, compare `need` and `have`; return true if they are equal.
Return false at the end.
approaches.why: O(1) updates per step, plus a 26-entry comparison per window.

approaches.name: Slide the window and track how many letters match
approaches.idea: Keep `diff[c] = need[c] − have[c]` and a counter of letters whose difference is 0. Only the letter entering and the one leaving change, so the counter updates in O(1); all 26 match exactly when the counter is 26.
steps: Set `diff[c] = count of c in s1` and `matches` = number of letters with `diff[c] == 0`.
For each index `i` of `s2`, the entering letter decreases its `diff`; adjust `matches` if that letter just became or just stopped being 0.
If `i >= n`, the leaving letter `s2[i − n]` increases its `diff`; adjust `matches` the same way.
Once the window has length n, return true if `matches == 26`. Return false at the end.
approaches.why: Each letter of each string is handled with O(1) work; the tables have a fixed 26 entries.

find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window with letter counts (anagram check)

approaches.name: Sort each window and compare
approaches.idea: A window is an anagram of `p` exactly when its sorted letters equal `p` sorted. Check every window of length `p.length`.
steps: Let `n = p.length`; sort the letters of `p`.
For each start `i` with `i + n <= s.length`, sort `s[i..i + n)` and compare with sorted `p`.
Collect every `i` that matches, in increasing order.
approaches.why: About m windows (m = `s.length`), each sorted in O(n log n); each sorted copy takes O(n) memory.

approaches.name: Slide a window of counts and compare all 26
approaches.idea: Keep letter counts of the current window and update them as it slides; compare them with the counts of `p` at each position.
steps: Count `p` into `need[26]`.
For each index `i` of `s`, add `s[i]` to `have`; if `i >= n`, remove `s[i − n]`.
When `i >= n − 1` and `have` equals `need`, record the start `i − n + 1`.
Return the recorded starts.
approaches.why: O(1) updates per step plus a 26-entry comparison per window (the output list aside).

approaches.name: Slide the window and count the letters still missing
approaches.idea: Keep `need[c]` = how many more of letter `c` the window still needs, and `missing` = the total still needed. A window is an anagram exactly when `missing == 0`, and each slide changes `missing` in O(1).
steps: Count `p` into `need`, and set `missing = p.length`.
For each index `i`: if `need[s[i]] > 0`, it fills a gap, so decrease `missing`; then decrease `need[s[i]]` (it may go negative: a surplus).
If `i >= n`, let the letter `s[i − n]` leave: increase its `need`; if it is now positive, a gap opened, so increase `missing`.
When `i >= n − 1` and `missing == 0`, record `i − n + 1`.
approaches.why: Each letter of `p` and `s` costs O(1); the count table has 26 entries (the output list aside).

minimum-window-substring.pattern: Variable-size sliding window: expand until valid, then shrink while still valid

approaches.name: From every start, extend until every needed letter is covered
approaches.idea: For each start, add letters until the window contains all of `t` (with repeats); that end gives the shortest valid window from this start.
steps: Count the letters of `t` and let `total = t.length`.
For each start `i`, copy the counts and set `missing = total`.
Move `j` right: if `s[j]` is still needed, decrease `missing`; decrease its count. When `missing == 0`, the window `s[i..j]` is valid: keep it if it is the shortest so far, and stop.
Return the shortest window, or `""`.
approaches.why: Each of the m starts may scan to the end of `s` (copying σ counts per start is O(σ) each, dominated by the scan). σ is the alphabet size, 52 letters here.

approaches.name: Sliding window with a count of missing letters
approaches.idea: Grow the window on the right until it covers `t` (`missing == 0`), then shrink it from the left for as long as it still covers `t`, recording the shortest valid window along the way.
steps: `need[c]` = how many more of `c` the window needs (starts as the counts of `t`); `missing = t.length`.
For each `r`: if `need[s[r]] > 0`, decrease `missing`; then decrease `need[s[r]]` (negative means a surplus).

While `missing == 0`: record the window `[l, r]` if it is the shortest; then remove `s[l]`: increase `need[s[l]]`, and if it becomes positive the window is short of that letter, so increase `missing`. Move `l` right.
Return the shortest recorded window, or `""`.
approaches.why: Counting `t` is O(n); each index of `s` enters and leaves the window once, O(m). The count table has one entry per possible character.

subarrays-with-k-different-integers.pattern: Sliding window counting trick: exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1)

approaches.name: From every start, extend while counting distinct values
approaches.idea: For each start, extend the subarray to the right, tracking how many distinct values it holds; count the ends where that number is exactly `k`, and stop once it exceeds `k`.
steps: For each start `i`, reset the counts and `distinct = 0`.
Move `j` right: if `nums[j]` is new, increase `distinct`.
If `distinct > k`, stop (longer subarrays only add values); if `distinct == k`, add 1 to the answer.
Return the answer.
approaches.why: Each start may scan to the end. The count table has one entry per possible value (values are at most n).

approaches.name: Count "at most k" twice and subtract
approaches.idea: "Exactly k distinct" is hard to slide, but "at most k distinct" is easy: for each right end `r`, every start from `l` to `r` works, adding `r − l + 1` subarrays. Then exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1).
steps: Write `atMost(k)`: a window `[l, r]` with value counts and a `distinct` counter.
For each `r`, add `nums[r]` (a new value increases `distinct`); while `distinct > k`, remove `nums[l]` and move `l` right.
Every subarray ending at `r` and starting in `[l, r]` has at most k distinct values: add `r − l + 1`.
Return `atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1)`.
approaches.why: Each `atMost` call moves both edges forward at most n times; it runs twice. The count table has n + 1 entries.
